title: One Leg, Zero Gravity: John McFall Could Redefine Who Goes to Space
summary: At 19, John McFall lay in a hospital bed, wondering if he'd ever walk again. A motorcycle accident had just cost him his right leg above the knee. Fast-forward 26 years, and McFall isn't just walking — he's sprinting toward a milestone no one has reached: becoming the first physically disabled person in space. McFall, now 45, is a British orthopedic surgeon, a former Paralympic bronze medalist in the 100-meter sprint, and a newly minted astronaut candidate. In 2022, he joined the European Space Agency's Fly! feasibility study, which aimed to determine whether a person with a physical disability could safely live and work on the International Space Station. Last year, he was medically cleared for a mission. Then, on June 2, the U.K. government announced he'd been selected as a prospective crew member for Haven-1, a commercial space station built by U.S. company Vast, slated to launch in early 2027. If all goes as planned, McFall will spend about 30 days in low Earth orbit, conducting experiments that could rewrite assumptions about disability in space. In an interview with Live Science, McFall was characteristically humble about the personal significance. "To me personally, it doesn't make a difference," he said. But he recognizes the broader impact: "The message it sends to wider society about what people are capable of — whether they have a disability or not — is very interesting and powerful." McFall and researchers are particularly curious about how his body will react to microgravity. He hypothesizes two potential benefits. First, because he has less lower-limb volume, the fluid shift that typically swells astronauts' optic disks — a condition called spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS), affecting 70-75% of crew members — might be proportionally smaller, reducing vision problems. Second, with lower bone mass, he might excrete less calcium, lowering the risk of kidney stones. But he's quick to emphasize these are just theories. "The real answer is, we don't know until we do the science," he said, referring to planned urine and blood samples and eye exams. Challenges remain unclear too. "Is having two legs useful in what we would call normal intravehicular operations?" he mused. During the feasibility study, the team couldn't identify a clear disadvantage — except maybe having to work a bit harder to stabilize himself. For now, McFall is focused on the mission ahead, not the history books. But if he floats through that hatch next year, he'll carry a powerful message: space is for everyone.
why_it_matters: McFall’s journey challenges outdated stereotypes about who can become an astronaut and, by extension, what any person with a disability can achieve in fields once thought off-limits. For middle schoolers, it sends a clear message that physical difference does not equal inability, and that pushing boundaries benefits all of society — not just the person breaking the barrier.

background_read: For decades, the world’s major space agencies, such as NASA and Russia’s Roscosmos, required astronauts to be in perfect physical health. People with disabilities were automatically excluded, based on the assumption that a 'standard' body was necessary for safety and performance.

That mindset started to shift more openly when the European Space Agency (ESA) — an intergovernmental organization of 22 European nations dedicated to space exploration — launched the Fly! feasibility study. Its goal was to test, for the first time, whether an astronaut with a physical disability could live and work aboard the International Space Station (ISS) without risk.

John McFall, a British orthopedic surgeon and former Paralympic bronze medalist in the 100-meter sprint, became the study's first candidate. He lost his right leg above the knee in a motorcycle accident at age 19, yet went on to build an elite athletic and medical career. He has now been selected as a prospective crew member for Haven-1, a commercial space station built by the U.S. company Vast, which plans to launch by early 2027.

His case fascinates scientists not just for what it says about inclusion, but also for what his body might reveal in microgravity. Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) — a swelling of the optic disk that blurs vision — hits most long-duration astronauts. McFall's lower-limb volume could change the fluid shift that triggers SANS, possibly offering a built-in protection. Such hypotheses, if confirmed, could reshape medical screening for future crews.

perspectives.description: McFall’s selection demonstrates that space agencies are finally recognizing the talent pool they’ve been ignoring. It inspires millions of people with disabilities and forces engineers to design spacecraft and suits that work for a wider range of bodies, potentially making space safer and more comfortable for everyone.

Some critics question whether the resources spent on a single disabled astronaut could be better used on missions with more predictable risk profiles. They worry that if a medical emergency were to occur in orbit, McFall’s unique physiology could complicate procedures, endangering the whole crew and setting back inclusive space policy.

This mission is a logical next step in the commercialization and diversification of spaceflight. As private companies like Vast build stations, they can afford to take calculated risks that government agencies historically avoided. Scientifically, McFall’s body is a natural experiment that could yield data on fluid shifts and bone metabolism that helps all astronauts.

If McFall succeeds, it could open the hatch for astronauts with a variety of disabilities, leading to a true 'space for all' ethos. Future habitats might be built with universal design principles, and space agencies may revise their medical certification rules. In the long run, a more diverse astronaut corps will be better equipped to handle the unknowns of long-duration Mars missions.
